documents.text:
October 30, 2026

Kimberly D. Bose, Secretary
Federal Energy Regulatory Commission
888 First Street, NE
Washington, DC 20426

Re:        Potomac Electric Power Company; Single Issue Depreciation Rate Filing
           Docket No. ER27-___-000

Dear Secretary Bose:

         Pursuant to Section 205 of the Federal Power Act (“FPA”), 1 and Part 35 of the
regulations of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (“Commission” ), 2 and Section 4.f.
of the Potomac Electric Power Company (“Pepco” or “Company”) Formula Rate
Implementation Protocols (“Implementation Protocols”) 3 authorizing a limited Section 205
filing, Pepco hereby respectfully submits for filing proposed revisions to the stated
depreciation rates contained in its formula transmission rate (“Formula Rate”) at Attachment
H-9A of the PJM OATT.4 Pepco requests that the proposed tariff sheets 5 be made effective
January 1, 2027.

       Based on an independent third-party depreciation study submitted with this filing, the
proposed depreciation rates will first be used for rate calculations in Pepco’s Formula Rate
annual update due May 15, 2027, for service on and after June 1, 2027, and is estimated to
increase Commission jurisdictional annual depreciation expense by approximately $6.8
million.

            I.          INFORMATION SUBMITTED WITH THIS FILING


1
    16 U.S.C. § 824d.

2
    18 C.F.R. Pt. 35.

3
    PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. (“PJM”) Open Access Transmission Tariff (“OATT”), Attachment H-9B.

4
  Pursuant to Order No. 714, this filing is submitted by PJM on behalf of Pepco as part of an XML filing package
that conforms with the Commission’s regulations. PJM has agreed to make all tariff filings on behalf of Pepco in
order to retain administrative control over the PJM OATT. Thus, Pepco has requested PJM to submit this filing in
the eTariff system as part of PJM’s electronic Intra PJM OATT.

5
 Specifically, the depreciation rates are at Attachment 12 of the Formula Rate. This filing revises only Attachment
12.

       This submission includes, along with this transmittal letter, the following documents:

           x     Attachment A: Redlined Tariff Attachment (PJM OATT Attachment H-9A – Pepco’s
                 Formula Rate Template) to be effective January 1, 2027;

           x     Attachment B: Clean Tariff Attachment (PJM OATT Attachment H-9A – Pepco’s
                 Formula Rate Template) to be effective January 1, 2027;

           x     Attachment C: Prepared Direct Testimony of Ned W. Allis and accompanying
                 exhibits; and

           x     Attachment D: Prepared Direct Testimony of Aristotelis K. Spanos and
                 accompanying exhibits.

           II.      BACKGROUND

           A. Description of Pepco

    Pepco, a District of Columbia and Virginia Corporation, is a wholly owned subsidiary of
Pepco Holdings, LLC, a public utility holding company. Pepco Holdings, LLC is a wholly
owned subsidiary of Exelon, a Pennsylvania corporation. Pepco owns approximately 12,000
miles of transmission and distribution facilities and provides delivered electric power to nearly
900,000 customers in the District of Columbia and Maryland. Pepco does not own any
generation facilities. Pepco’s retail electric service is regulated by the Maryland Public Service
Commission and the Public Service Commission of the District of Columbia, while PJM’s
provision of transmission service over Pepco’s transmission facilities and sales for resale of
electric energy in interstate commerce are regulated by this Commission.

           B. Pepco’s Formula Rate Depreciation Provision

        Pepco’s transmission Formula Rate, which originated from a March 20, 2006 Settlement
Agreement and Offer of Settlement was approved by Commission order issued on April 19,
2006.6 In 2019, Pepco submitted revisions to the Formula Rate and Implementation Protocols to
establish a forward-looking formula rate and adjust the Company’s reconciliation (or “true up”)
mechanism to better align incurrence of actual transmission costs with recovery of those costs
through rates. Eventually, the proceeding resulted in a settlement with a revised Formula Rate
and Implementation Protocols.7

       Under the current Formula Rate and Implementation Protocols, an annual update is
required by May 15th of each year to be effective each June 1st. As part of the update, the
formula template is populated to calculate projected rates for the upcoming year, and a true-up of


6
    Baltimore Gas and Elec. Co., 115 FERC ¶ 61,066 (2006).

7
    PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 172 FERC ¶ 61,271 (2020).


                                                        2
 prior year rates is calculated, using the most current Form 1 data submitted by Pepco. Pepco
follows this update procedure each year, with its next update due by May 15, 2027.

        Pepco’s depreciation schedule, Attachment 12 of its Formula Rate, was revised in 2020
by a settlement in Docket No. ER19-10, which added a footnote providing that the depreciation
rates be updated at least every five years. 8 Specifically, footnote 2 of Formula Rate Attachment
12 provides: “Within five years of the effective date of the Settlement in Docket No. ER19-5 et
al, and at least every five years thereafter, Pepco will file an FPA Section 205 rate proceeding,
with a new depreciation study, to revise its transmission depreciation rates (unless the company
has otherwise submitted an FPA Section 205 rate filing, with a new depreciation study, that
addresses its depreciation rates in the prior five years).”

       Pepco’s most recent depreciation rate filing, before this one, was its filing on October 9,
2020 in Docket No. ER21-83. The rates were set for hearing and ultimately agreed depreciation
rates were adopted in a 2022 settlement.9

        As specified in the Implementation Protocols, Pepco’s depreciation rates are “stated
values to be used in the rate formula until changed pursuant to an FPA Section 205 … filing.” 10
The Implementation Protocols further provide that Pepco may make a limited, single issue filing
pursuant to Section 205 to modify the stated values in the formula rate for depreciation rates. 11

8
    Settlement approved at Commonwealth Edison Co., et al, 172 FERC ¶ 61,272 (2020).

9
 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 180 FERC ¶ 61,100 (2022). While preparing this filing, it was discovered that in a
2024 filing in Docket No. ER25-144 addressing Order No. 898 compliance, the Company inadvertently substituted
an outdated pre-settlement version of Attachment 12 and its depreciation rates into the tariff, with an effective date
of January 1, 2025. Pepco had no intent in 2024 to alter the depreciation rates from those it had settled – the
outdated attachment was an inadvertent error. In annual updates submitted by Pepco, Pepco has continued to use the
settlement depreciation rates, and in the attached redline, the base tariff version that is used is the settled version of
Attachment 12.

If the Commission concludes the tariff sheets should be corrected, we suggest that Pepco be directed to make a
clean-up filing that will fix the depreciation schedule to the settled and accepted schedule that should be in place, for
the period January 1, 2025 until the effective date of the new revisions proposed in this filing.

An alternative approach to retroactively revising the erroneous tariff sheets, would be to grant Pepco waivers
permitting Pepco to continue to rely on the settlement depreciation rates from January 1, 2025 through the effective
date of the new revisions in this filing. The Commission grants limited waivers of tariff provisions where: “(1) the
underlying error was made in good faith; (2) the waiver is of limited scope; (3) the waiver addresses a concrete
problem; and (4) the waiver does not have undesirable consequences, such as harming third parties.” AEP
Generation Resources, Inc., 170 FERC ¶ 61,103, at P 14 (2020). Here, the underlying error was made in good faith
and unintentional. The waiver is of limited scope, relating only to depreciation rates for the years 2025 and 2026.
The waiver addresses a concrete problem that the effective tariff does not reflect the 2022 settlement. And the
waiver would not have undesirable consequences – customers benefit from the lower settlement depreciation rates,
and customers were on notice of the settlement rates, because they were agreed to in settlement and then accepted by
the Commission. In the circumstances, waiver is appropriate.

10

11

             III.     EXPLANATION OF PROPOSED CHANGES

                     A. Timing of this Filing

        As discussed above, Pepco’s last depreciation case was filed October 9, 2020 in Docket
No. ER21-83, and the rates were then revised in 2022 as a result of settlement discussions. The
current rates are thus only four years old – but Formula Rate Attachment 12, Footnote 2 provides
that the depreciation rates should be refiled within five years of the last Section 205 filing –
which would imply five years from the 2020 filing date of Docket No. ER21-83 rather than five
years from the 2022 settlement filing in that docket. This proceeding should have been filed by
October 9, 2025.

       It was an oversight by Pepco that led to this filing being made approximately a year late.
Fortunately, customers were not injured. As discussed below, the revised depreciation rates will
increase depreciation charged to jurisdictional rates by approximately $6.8 million per year; this
means that customers benefited from the delayed filing by Pepco, which will lead to rates being
updated a year later than otherwise.

                     B. Derivation of Proposed Revised Deprecation Rates

         Depreciation rates change over time due to numerous factors including, among others,
changes in technology, updates to operational practices, which may shorten or extend the useful
life of property, changes in the mix of assets within a composite depreciable group, variances in
estimated removal costs and salvage recoveries versus actual amounts. 12 The purpose of this
filing is to adjust Pepco’s transmission depreciation rates pursuant to Section 205 to reflect
revisions in accordance with the depreciation study prepared by Ned W. Allis, Senior Vice
President of Gannett Fleming Valuation and Rate Consultants, LLC., an independent third-party
depreciation expert (“Depreciation Study”). The Depreciation Study is included among the
exhibits sponsored by Witness Allis.

         The Depreciation Study analyzes annual transmission depreciation rates based on
Pepco’s depreciable plant in service as of December 31,2025. 13 As explained by Witness Allis,
the recommended annual depreciation accrual rates were developed by first estimating the
service life and net salvage characteristics for each depreciable property group (i.e., each plant
account or subaccount identified as having similar characteristics) and then calculating the
composite remaining lives and annual depreciation accrual rates based on the service life and net
salvage estimates.14 Witness Allis is also sponsoring an exhibit that provides a breakdown of the




12
     Spanos Direct Testimony, Attachment D at 4:7-11.

13
     Allis Direct Testimony, Attachment C at 3:11-16.

14
     Id., Attachment C at 5-21.


                                                        4
 depreciation rates by FERC plant account number and compares the existing and proposed
annual deprecation accrual rates.15

The Depreciation Study results in an overall increase in depreciation expense of approximately
$6.8 million primarily due to higher depreciation rates for Account 352, Structures and
Improvements, Account 353, Station Equipment, Account 354, Towers and Fixtures, and
Account 357, Underground Conduit.16 Generally, the higher depreciation rates for these
accounts are the result of increased negative net salvage value. 17 Across the industry, net salvage
has trended more negative reflecting higher labor costs, increased work requirements, more
stringent safety and environmental requirements, equipment costs, more complex permitting and
traffic control, and work in congested or constrained locations. 18 Accordingly, the results of the
Depreciation Study are generally consistent with these industry trends.

         In addition to the depreciation rates for transmission plant, this filing proposes
depreciation rates for general and intangible plant. As explained by witness Allis, those rates
were the subject of separate depreciation studies that he performed, yielding rates that he
recommends.19 The general and intangible rates also have been subject to litigation in Pepco’s
retail proceedings in Maryland and the District of Columbia. To ensure alignment of retail and
wholesale ratemaking, the general and intangible rates have been revised to the levels ultimately
approved and then implemented in those retail jurisdictions. 20

               A. Implementation of Revised Deprecation Rates Under Pepco’s Formula Rate

        To further support Pepco’s request to modify its transmission depreciation rates, Pepco is
also submitting the testimony and associated exhibits of Aristotelis K. Spanos, Manager,
Revenue Requirements for Pepco Holdings, LLC (PHI).

       Witness Spanos describes how Pepco will implement the revised stated rates under its
Formula Rate. Though the revised depreciation rates become effective January 1, 2027, he
explains that Pepco will first use them in rate calculations in an annual update to its formula
transmission rate in May 2027, setting new rate levels for service on and after June 1, 2027. 21
That update includes a projection of calendar year 2027, and that projection will include the new

 depreciation rates.22 The transmission rate charged for the following year will then be subject to
a true-up in the May 2028 annual update, based on 2027 actuals. 23

            IV.      LIST OF PERSONS RECEIVING A COPY OF THIS FILING

         On behalf of Pepco, PJM has served a copy of this filing on behalf of all PJM Members
and on all state utility regulatory commissions in the PJM Region by posting this filing
electronically. In accordance with the Commission’s regulations, 24 PJM will post a copy of this
filing to the FERC filings section of its internet site, located at the following link:
https://www.pjm.com/library/filing-order with a specific link to the new-filed document, and will
send an e-mail on the same date as this filing to all PJM Members and all state utility regulatory
commissions in the PJM Region25 alerting them that this filing has been made by PJM and is
available by following such link. If the document is not immediately available through the
referenced link, the document will be available through the referenced link within 24 hours of the
filing. Also, a copy of this filing will be available on the Commission’s eLibrary website located
at the following link: https://elibrary.ferc.gov/ in accordance with the Commission’s regulations
and Order No. 714.

       Additionally, a copy of this filing is being served directly by Pepco on representatives of
the Maryland Public Service Commission, Maryland Office of the People’s Counsel, the Public
Service Commission of the District of Columbia, and District of Columbia Office of People’s
Counsel, and is also available for public inspection, during regular business hours, in convenient
form and place, at the offices of Pepco.

            V.       OTHER FILING REQUIREMENTS

        None of the costs proposed to be recovered in proposed tariff sheets have been alleged or
judged in any administrative or judicial proceeding to be illegal, duplicative, or unnecessary
costs that are demonstrably the product of discriminatory employment practices. 26

            VI.      REQUESTED EFFECTIVE DATE AND DESIGNATION

        Pepco requests that the enclosed proposed tariff sheets be included in Attachment H-9A
of the PJM OATT effective January 1, 2027 without suspension, or with a nominal one-day

22
  Id. To be clear, the May 2027 update will also include a true-up of calendar year 2026 for service taken June 1,
2026 through May 31, 2027. The 2026 true-up portion of the update will use the depreciation rates applicable to
2026. Id.

23
     Id.

24
     See 18 C.F.R. §§ 35.2(e) and 385.2010(f)(3).

25
  PJM already maintains, updates, and regularly uses e-mail lists for all PJM members and affected state
commissions.

26
     18 C.F.R. 35.13(b)(7)(2025).


                                                         6
 suspension period, with the understanding that the depreciation rate change requested herein will
not be reflected in billings until Pepco submits its annual formula rate update setting rate levels
for service on and after June 1, 2027.

        VII.    COST OF SERVICE, REVENUE INFORMATION, AND REQUEST FOR
                WAIVERS

         As no cost of service or rate design change is being made as part of this filing, Pepco
requests that the Commission find good cause to waive Section 35.13 of the Commission’s
regulations, 18 C.F.R. § 35.13, including any requirement that the filing contain Statements AA
through BM in support of the filing; any Period I-Period II data requirements, and any
requirement in Section 35.13(a)(2)(iv) to determine if and the extent to which a proposed change
constitutes a rate increase based on Period I-Period II rates and billing determinants. In addition,
Pepco hereby respectfully requests a waiver, to the extent one is deemed necessary, of the
requirement that it file an attestation pursuant to 18 C.F.R. § 35.13(d) as inapplicable under the
circumstances presented here, inasmuch as there are no costs contained in this filing to be
attested to by any corporate official.

        Although Pepco has not identified any additional waivers of the Commission’s
Regulations that are necessary to permit this filing to be granted, Pepco further requests that the
Commission grant any additional waivers of its rules and regulations it may deem necessary to
approve this rate application by the requested effective date.

        VIII. NOTICE AND CORRESPONDENCE

       Correspondence, pleadings and other materials regarding this filing should be
addressed to the following persons:

         IX.    CONCLUSION

        For all the reasons set forth herein, Pepco respectfully request that the Commission
accept for filing its proposed revised PJM OATT Attachment H-9A, reflecting revised
depreciation rates, effective January 1, 2027 with no suspension or hearing, or with at most a
nominal one-day suspension period.

                  This section is used to calculate the projected deficient / (excess) ADIT balances. The computations in columns A-H of this workpaper apply the proration rules of Reg. Sec. 1.167(l)-1(h)(6) to the projected annual
                  activity of deficient / (excess) accumulated deferred income taxes subject to the normalization requirements . Activity related to the portions of the account balances not subject to the proration requirement are
     A            averaged instead of prorated. For deficient / (excess) accumulated deferred income taxes subject to the normalization requirements, projected activity for months prior to the future portion of the test period is
                  averaged rather than prorated.




                  This section is used to calculate the actual deficient / (excess) ADIT balances. The computations in columns A-M of this workpaper apply the proration rules of Reg. Sec. 1.167(l)-1(h)(6) and averaging in
                  accordance with IRC Section 168(i)(9)(B) consistency requirement to the actual annual activity of deficient / (excess) accumulated deferred income taxes subject to the normalization requirements. Differences
     B            attributable to over-projection of deficient / (excess) ADIT amortization in the projected revenue requirement will result in a proportionate reversal of the projected prorated deficient / (excess) ADIT activity in the
                  true-up adjustment to the extent of the over-projection. Differences attributable to under-projection of deficient / (excess) ADIT in the projected revenue requirement will result in an adjustment to the projected
                  prorated ADIT activity by 50 percent of the difference between the projected monthly activity and the actual monthly activity. However, when projected monthly deficient / (excess) ADIT activity is an increase and
                  actual monthly deficient / (excess) ADIT activity is a decrease, 50 percent of the actual monthly deficient / (excess) ADIT activity will be used. Likewise, when projected monthly deficient / (excess) ADIT activity is a
                  decrease and actual monthly deficient / (excess) ADIT activity is an increase, 50 percent of actual monthly deficient / (excess) ADIT activity will be used. This section is used to calculate deficient / (excess) ADIT
                  activity in the true-up adjustment only. For deficient / (excess) accumulated deferred income taxes subject to the normalization requirements, actual activity for months prior to the future portion of the test period is
                  averaged rather than prorated.

     C            negative, a negative in Column (J) represents under-projection (excess of actual activity over projected activity) and a positive in Column (J) represents over-projection (amount of projected activity that did not

ATTACHMENT C

Prepared Direct Testimony
     of Ned W Allis
      (and exhibits)
                                                                                      Attachment C
                                                                                     Witness Allis


                             UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                    BEFORE THE
                      FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION
                          DIRECT TESTIMONY OF NED W. ALLIS
                               DOCKET NO. ER27-____-000
 1
 2                                          I. Introduction
 3
 4   Q1.   Please state your name and business address.

 5   A1.          My name is Ned W. Allis. My business address is 300 Sterling Parkway,

 6         Mechanicsburg, Pennsylvania 17050.

 7   Q2.   By whom and in what capacity are you employed?

 8   A2.          I am employed by Gannett Fleming Valuation and Rate Consultants, LLC

 9         (“Gannett Fleming”), part of GFT Infrastructure, Inc. (“GFT”), where I am Senior Vice

10         President. I am responsible for conducting depreciation, valuation and original cost

11         studies, determining service life and net salvage estimates, conducting field reviews,

12         presenting recommended depreciation rates to clients, and supporting such rates before

13         state and federal regulatory agencies. I am also responsible for Gannett Fleming’s

14         proprietary depreciation software, training of depreciation staff, and the development of

15         solutions for technical issues related to depreciation.

16   Q3.   What is your educational background?

17   A3.          I have Bachelor of Science degree in Mathematics from Lafayette College in

18         Easton, PA.

19   Q4.   Do you belong to any professional societies?

20   A4.          Yes. I am a member of the Society of Depreciation Professionals (“Society”) and

21         an associate member of the American Gas Association/Edison Electric Institute




                                                    1
                                                                                       Attachment C
                                                                                      Witness Allis
 1         (“AGA/EEI”), an industry accounting committee. I am a past president of the Society

 2         and currently serve as an instructor for depreciation training sponsored by the Society.

 3   Q5.   Do you hold any special certification as a depreciation expert?

 4   A5.          Yes. The Society of Depreciation Professionals has established national standards

 5         for depreciation professionals. The Society administers an examination to become

 6         certified in this field. I passed the certification exam in September 2011 and was

 7         recertified in March 2017 and January 2022.

 8   Q6.   Have you received any additional education relating to utility plant depreciation?

 9   A6.          Yes. I have completed the following courses conducted by the Society of

10         Depreciation Professionals: “Depreciation Basics,” “Life and Net Salvage Analysis” and

11         “Preparing and Defending Depreciation Study”.

12   Q7.   Please outline your experience in the field of depreciation.

13   A7.          I joined Gannett Fleming in October 2006 as an Analyst. My duties included

14         assembling basic data required for depreciation studies, conducting statistical analyses of

15         service life and net salvage data, calculating annual and accrued depreciation, assisting

16         in preparing reports and assisting in providing testimony setting forth and defending the

17         results of the studies. I also developed and maintained Gannett Fleming’s proprietary

18         depreciation software. In March 2013, I was promoted to the position of Supervisor,

19         Depreciation Studies. In March 2017, I was promoted to Project Manager, Depreciation

20         and Technical Development. In January 2019, I was promoted to Vice President. In

21         November 2025, I was promoted to my current position of Senior Vice President.




                                                   2
                                                                                          Attachment C
                                                                                         Witness Allis
 1   Q8.    Have you previously testified before the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission

 2          (“Commission”)?

 3   A8.             Yes.

 4   Q9.    Have you submitted testimony in any other jurisdictions?

 5   A9.             Yes. I have testified on depreciation-related issues in more than twenty U.S.

 6          regulatory jurisdictions, including the Commission. In addition to submitting testimony

 7          in these jurisdictions, I have also assisted other witnesses in the preparation of direct and

 8          rebuttal testimony in numerous other states and two Canadian provinces. Exhibit C-1

 9          provides a list of depreciation cases in which I have submitted testimony.

10   Q10. What is the purpose of your pre-filed direct testimony in this proceeding?

11   A10.            I was asked to recommend depreciation rates for Potomac Electric Power

12          Company (“Pepco” or “Company”) transmission plant accounts. I am sponsoring Exhibit

13          C-2, which provides the results of my depreciation analysis related to Pepco electric

14          transmission plant as of December 31, 2025 (“the Depreciation Study” or “Study”). The

15          recommended depreciation rates in my study for Pepco are set forth on Table 1 on page

16          VI-4 of the Study.

17   Q11. Please summarize your testimony.

18   A11.            My testimony explains the methods and procedures of the Depreciation Study

19          and sets forth the annual depreciation rates as of December 31, 2025 for transmission

20          plant.   Exhibit C-2, which is the Depreciation Study, sets in detail the methods,

21          procedures and results of the Depreciation Study as of December 31, 2025.                My




                                                     3
                                                                                        Attachment C
                                                                                       Witness Allis
 1          Depreciation Study will be explained in Part II of this testimony. The results of the Study

 2          will be explained in Part III of this testimony.

 3   Q12. Please summarize the principal conclusion of your depreciation study.

 4   A12.          The principal conclusion of the Study is that Pepco’s current depreciation rates

 5          should be updated to reflect the results of the Depreciation Study. Generally, my

 6          recommended rates are based on a combination of my review of Pepco’s historical data

 7          and operating practices, as well as the application of informed judgment that incorporates

 8          factors such as general knowledge of the property studied, information obtained from site

 9          visits and meetings with Company personnel, and service life and net salvage estimates

10          of other electric utilities. Exhibit C-3 sets forth a comparison of the proposed rates with

11          the current rates as of December 31, 2025.

12                 As of December 31, 2025, the recommended depreciation rates result in an

13          increase in depreciation expense of approximately $6.8 million, when compared to the

14          depreciation expense that results from the current depreciation rates as reflected in

15          Exhibit C-3.

16                 The increase in depreciation expense was primarily driven by the increase in rate

17          for Account 353, Station Equipment. For many accounts, including Accounts 352 and

18          354 through 358, the higher depreciation rates are associated with more negative net

19          salvage estimates.

20

21                            II. Methods Used in the Depreciation Study

22   Q13. Please define the concept of depreciation.




                                                     4
                                                                                          Attachment C
                                                                                         Witness Allis
 1   A13.           The Commission’s Uniform System of Accounts (“USOA”) defines depreciation

 2          as follows:

 3                           Depreciation, as applied to depreciable electric plant, means the loss in
 4                           service value not restored by current maintenance, incurred in connection
 5                           with the consumption or prospective retirement of electric plant in the
 6                           course of service from causes which are known to be in current operation
 7                           and against which the utility is not protected by insurance. Among the
 8                           causes to be given consideration are wear and tear, decay, action of the
 9                           elements, inadequacy, obsolescence, changes in the art, changes in
10                           demand and requirements of public authorities.1

11   Q14. What is the purpose of a depreciation study?

12   A14            The purpose of a depreciation study is to recommend depreciation rates to be used

13          for book and ratemaking purposes. The study recommends service life and net salvage

14          estimates for each depreciable group (e.g., a plant account), which are used to calculate

15          depreciation rates based on plant and reserve balances as of the test year of the study

16          (e.g.., December 31, 2025 for the current study).

17   Q15    In preparing the depreciation study, did you follow generally accepted practices in

18          the field of depreciation?

19   A15.           Yes. The methods and procedures used to estimate service lives and net salvage

20          and to calculate depreciation are widely accepted practices in the utility industry.

21   Q16. Please describe the contents of your report.

22   A16.           The Study is presented in nine parts:

23                  •     Part I, Introduction, presents the scope and basis for the Depreciation Study;

24                  •     Part II, Estimation of Survivor Curves, explains the process of estimating




     1      18 C.F.R. 101 (Uniform System of Accounts), Definition 12.




                                                         5
                                                                                      Attachment C
                                                                                     Witness Allis
 1                    survivor curves and the retirement rate method of life analysis;

 2                •   Part III, Service Life Considerations, discusses factors and the informed

 3                    judgment involved with the estimation of service life;

 4                •   Part IV, Net Salvage Considerations, discusses factors and the informed

 5                    judgment involved with the estimation of net salvage;

 6                •   Part V, Calculation of Annual and Accrued Depreciation, explains the

 7                    method, procedure and technique used in the calculation of annual

 8                    depreciation expense and the theoretical reserve;

 9                •   Part VI, Results of Study, sets forth the service life estimates, net salvage

10                    estimates, and annual depreciation rates and accruals for each depreciable

11                    group. This section also includes a description of the detailed tabulations

12                    supporting the Depreciation Study. Additionally, this section includes the

13                    depreciation rates and accruals resulting from using different net salvage

14                    methods;

15                •   Part VII, Service Life Statistics, sets forth the survivor curve estimates and

16                    original life tables for each plant account and subaccount;

17                •   Part VIII, Net Salvage Statistics, sets forth the net salvage analysis for each

18                    plant account and subaccount; and

19                •   Part IX, Detailed Depreciation Calculations, sets forth the calculation of

20                    average remaining life for each property group.

21   Q17. Please identify the depreciation method that you used.




                                                   6
                                                                                         Attachment C
                                                                                        Witness Allis
 1   A17.          I used the straight line remaining life method of depreciation (also referred to as

 2          the straight line method and remaining life technique), with the average service life

 3          procedure. This method of depreciation aims to distribute the unrecovered cost of fixed

 4          capital assets over the estimated remaining useful life of each unit or group of assets in a

 5          systematic and rational manner and has been used in many depreciation studies before

 6          the Commission.

 7   Q18. Did you review prior Commission filings on Pepco’s depreciation accrual rates?

 8   A18.          Yes. Pepco’s current depreciation rates for electric transmission plant were

 9          adopted and implicitly accepted in the Company’s most recent formula rate filing in

10          Docket No. ER21-83.

11   Q19. What are your recommended annual depreciation accrual rates for Pepco?

12   A19.          My recommended annual depreciation accrual rates as of December 31, 2025 for

13          Pepco are set forth in Exhibit C-3 and on Table 1 on page VI-4 of the Depreciation Study,

14          Exhibit C-2.

15   Q20. How did you determine the recommended annual depreciation accrual rates?

16   A20.          I did this in two phases. In the first phase, I estimated the service life and net

17          salvage characteristics for each depreciable group (i.e., each plant account or subaccount

18          identified as having similar characteristics). In the second phase, I calculated the

19          composite remaining lives and annual depreciation accrual rates based on the service life

20          estimates and net salvage estimates.

21   Q21. Please describe the first phase of the Depreciation Study, in which you estimated

22          the service life characteristics for each depreciable group.




                                                     7
                                                                                         Attachment C
                                                                                        Witness Allis
 1   A21.          The service life and net salvage study consisted of compiling historic data from

 2          records related to Pepco’s plant; analyzing these data to obtain historic trends of survivor

 3          characteristics; obtaining supplementary information from management and operating

 4          personnel concerning practices and plans as they relate to plant operations; and

 5          interpreting the above data and the estimates used by other electric utilities to form

 6          judgments of average service life characteristics.

 7   Q22. What historic data did you analyze for the purpose of estimating service life

 8          characteristics?

 9   A22.          I analyzed the Company’s accounting entries that record plant transactions during

10          the 26-year period from 1999 through 2025. The transactions included additions,

11          retirements, transfers and the related balances. The Company records also included

12          surviving dollar value by year installed for each plant account as of December 31, 2025.

13          The vintage years (or ages) of retirements were available from 2005 through 2025. For

14          the years prior to 2005, for which the vintage years of retirements were unavailable, the

15          total annual retirements by account were statistically aged. This allowed for a longer

16          period of data to be available for the life analysis than if only the recorded aged

17          retirements were used.

18   Q23. What method did you use to analyze this service life data?

19   A23.          I used the retirement rate method for all accounts. This is the most appropriate

20          method when aged retirement data are available, because it determines the average rates

21          of retirement actually experienced by the Company during the period covered by the




                                                     8
                                                                                           Attachment C
                                                                                          Witness Allis
 1          study. For the study, bands of years were considered that included the full range of data

 2          available (aged and statistically aged) as well as bands with only recorded aged data.

 3   Q24. Please explain how you used the retirement rate method to analyze Pepco’s service

 4          life data.

 5   A24.           I applied the retirement rate method to each different group of property in the

 6          study. For each property group, I used the retirement rate method to form a life table

 7          which, when plotted, shows an original survivor curve for that property group. Each

 8          original survivor curve represents the average survivor pattern experienced by the several

 9          vintage groups during the experience band studied.           The survivor patterns do not

10          necessarily describe the life characteristics of the property group; therefore, interpretation

11          of the original survivor curves is required in order to use them as valid considerations in

12          estimating service life. The Iowa-type survivor curves were used to perform these

13          interpretations.

14   Q25. What is an “Iowa-type survivor curve” and how did you use such curves to estimate

15          the service life characteristics for each property group?

16   A25.           Iowa-type curves are a widely used group of generalized survivor curves that

17          contain the range of survivor characteristics usually experienced by utilities and other

18          industrial companies. The Iowa curves were developed at the Iowa State University

19          College of Engineering Experiment Station through an extensive process of observing

20          and classifying the ages at which various types of property used by utilities and other

21          industrial companies had been retired.




                                                      9
                                                                                           Attachment C
                                                                                          Witness Allis
 1                  Iowa-type curves are used to smooth and extrapolate original survivor curves

 2          determined by the retirement rate method. The Iowa curves and truncated Iowa curves

 3          were used in this study to describe the forecasted rates of retirement based on the

 4          observed rates of retirement and the outlook for future retirements.

 5                  The estimated survivor curve designations for each depreciable property group

 6          indicate the average service life, the family within the Iowa system to which the property

 7          group belongs, and the relative height of the mode. For example, the Iowa 50-R2

 8          indicates an average service life of fifty years; a right-moded, or R, type curve (the mode

 9          occurs after average life for right-moded curves); and a moderate height, 2, for the mode

10          (possible modes for R type curves range from 1 to 5, not including half mode curves such

11          as the R0.5).

12   Q26. Should the estimation of survivor curves be based solely on the mathematical results

13          of statistical life analyses?

14   A26.          No. Because depreciation requires the estimation of future service lives for assets

15          currently in service, and because the historical database only allows for the analysis of a

16          portion of the full service lives of each group of assets, informed judgment is necessary

17          to determine the most reasonable survivor curve estimate. Judgment must be used not

18          only to incorporate information external to the statistical analyses, but also to properly

19          interpret the historical data as part of the curve fitting process. Authoritative depreciation

20          texts support that judgment is necessary in the estimation of depreciation, and that

21          reliance only on statistical results can, and does, produce unreasonable results.




                                                     10
                                                                                         Attachment C
                                                                                        Witness Allis
 1   Q27. How do you determine the appropriate survivor curve when the statistical analysis

 2          indicates that more than one curve may reasonably describe the historical data?

 3   A27.           The objective of the analysis is not simply to identify the Iowa curve that produces

 4          the lowest mathematical measure of error. The historical analysis describes the retirement

 5          experience observed during the period studied, while the depreciation estimate must

 6          reflect the expected future retirement characteristics of the property currently in service.

 7          Accordingly, I consider the mathematical and visual fit of alternative survivor curves, the

 8          amount of property exposed to retirement at the various ages, the consistency of the

 9          results across different experience bands, and information concerning the nature of the

10          property and the Company’s expected future operations.

11                  Particular care is required when interpreting the later ages of an original survivor

12          curve. At those ages, the amount of property exposed to retirement may be substantially

13          smaller than at earlier ages, and individual transactions can therefore have a greater

14          influence on the indicated survivor pattern. I do not disregard those observations. Rather,

15          I consider them in the context of the amount of exposure supporting the observations and

16          the other information available for the property group. My recommended survivor curves

17          reflect my judgment as to the retirement pattern that best represents the property over its

18          full expected service life.

19   Q28. How do you evaluate an account where the historical data reflect relatively few

20          retirements?

21   A28.           A history of relatively few retirements is relevant evidence and generally

22          indicates that the property is capable of providing service for a relatively long period.




                                                    11
                                                                                        Attachment C
                                                                                       Witness Allis
 1          However, limited retirement activity also means that the available historical data may not

 2          describe the complete retirement pattern of the property. If a substantial portion of the

 3          property remains in service, the ultimate ages at which those assets will be retired have

 4          not yet been observed.

 5                  For that reason, I do not assume either that the historical absence of retirements

 6          will continue indefinitely or that a particular level of future retirements must occur at a

 7          specified age. I consider the historical experience together with the age and

 8          characteristics of the surviving property, the function of the assets, Company plans and

 9          operating practices, field observations, and experience with comparable electric utility

10          property. The resulting survivor curve is intended to provide a reasonable forecast of the

11          entire retirement distribution, including the portion that cannot yet be observed in the

12          historical data.

13   Q29. Have you physically observed Pepco’s assets as part of your depreciation studies?

14   A29.           Yes. A field review of Pepco’s property was completed in April 2019 and in

15          August 2026. Field reviews are conducted to become familiar with Company operations

16          and obtain an understanding of the function of the plant and information with respect to

17          the reasons for past retirements and the expected future causes of retirements. This

18          knowledge as well as information from other discussions with management was

19          incorporated into my statistical analyses.

20   Q30. How did your experience performing or participating in other depreciation studies

21          affect your work in this case?




                                                    12
                                                                                         Attachment C
                                                                                        Witness Allis
 1   A30.           Because I customarily conduct field reviews for depreciation studies, I have had

 2          the opportunity to visit many similar facilities and meet with operations personnel at

 3          other companies. The knowledge accumulated from those visits and meetings provide

 4          me useful information that I can draw on to confirm or challenge my numerical analyses

 5          concerning plant condition and remaining life estimates.

 6   Q31. What information concerning Pepco’s current operations and future plans did you

 7          consider in estimating service lives?

 8   A31.           In addition to the statistical analyses and my observations during the field

 9          reviews, I considered Pepco’s current transmission operations, planned capital projects,

10          and the principal drivers of transmission investment. This information is relevant because

11          transmission assets may be retired for reasons other than physical deterioration or failure.

12          Assets may also be replaced or retired as a result of capacity requirements, reliability

13          needs, system reconfiguration, changes in voltage, obsolescence, or the reconstruction of

14          existing facilities.

15                  Pepco is undertaking several significant transmission initiatives. The Capital Grid

16          program includes development of a 230 kV backbone and loop into the District of

17          Columbia, including Gas Insulated Substation (“GIS”) at Takoma, reconstruction of 230

18          kV facilities to Takoma, reconstruction of the Harvard and Champlain substations, a new

19          substation at Mt. Vernon, a connection to the new Waterfront substation, and two 230

20          kV lines. Capacity expansion and reliability are important drivers of this work.

21                  The Downtown Resupply program includes new 69 kV transmission facilities and

22          is expected to result in system refeeds and retirements. In a number of instances, existing




                                                    13
                                                                                        Attachment C
                                                                                       Witness Allis
 1          13 kV facilities will be replaced with 69 kV facilities. This work is being driven by

 2          capacity requirements as well as the age and condition of existing facilities, including

 3          older pipe filled cable.

 4                  Other transmission investment includes circuit rebuilds driven by age, condition

 5          and capacity; refurbishment of tower lines due to age and condition; condition based

 6          replacement of transmission tower foundations; and replacement of ACSR static wire

 7          that is susceptible to corrosion and early failure. Pepco is also experiencing additional

 8          PJM driven transmission work associated with load growth and large loads, including

 9          potential upgrades to existing transmission lines to provide additional capacity.

10                  I considered these projects and investment drivers together with Pepco’s

11          historical retirement experience in developing my service life estimates. The historical

12          data provide important evidence concerning the service realized by Pepco’s transmission

13          assets to date, while the current transmission investment program provides information

14          concerning the circumstances that may cause assets presently in service to be retired in

15          the future.

16   Q32. Why is it important to consider these different sources of information together when

17          estimating service lives?

18   A32.           Depreciation is inherently prospective. Historical retirement data provide

19          objective evidence of the service realized by the Company’s property, but they

20          necessarily reflect past experience and, in many cases, only a portion of the ultimate life

21          cycle of property that remains in service. Statistical curve fitting therefore cannot, by

22          itself, determine the future retirement pattern.




                                                     14
                                                                                          Attachment C
                                                                                         Witness Allis
 1                 For that reason, I consider the statistical analyses together with the amount of

 2          property exposed to retirement at different ages, the age and composition of the surviving

 3          property, information concerning Company operations and future plans, observations

 4          from field reviews, and experience with similar property at other electric utilities. I do

 5          not rely on any one of these considerations in isolation. The recommended survivor curve

 6          represents my judgment based on the combined weight of the available evidence. This

 7          approach is also consistent with the methodology already described in the draft testimony

 8   Q33. Please explain the concept of “net salvage.”

 9   A33.          Net salvage is a component of the service value of capital assets that is

10          traditionally recovered through depreciation rates. The service value of an asset is its

11          original cost less its net salvage. Net salvage is the salvage value received for the asset

12          upon retirement less the cost to retire the asset. When the cost to retire exceeds the

13          salvage value, the result is negative net salvage.

14                 Inasmuch as depreciation expense is the loss in service value of an asset during a

15          defined period, e.g., one year, it should include a ratable portion of both the original cost

16          and the net salvage. That is, the net salvage related to an asset should be incorporated in

17          the cost of service during the same period as its original cost so that customers receiving

18          service from the asset pay rates that include a portion of both elements of the asset’s

19          service value, the original cost and the net salvage value.

20                 For example, the full recovery of the service value of a $1,000 pole may include

21          not only the $1,000 of original cost, but also, on average, $450 to remove the pole at the

22          end of its life and $50 in salvage value. In this example, the net salvage component is




                                                     15
                                                                                        Attachment C
                                                                                       Witness Allis
 1          negative $400 ($50 - $450), and the net salvage percent is negative 40% (($50 -

 2          $450)/$1,000).

 3   Q34. Please explain how the net salvage estimates were determined based on the

 4          traditional method.

 5   A34.          I estimated the net salvage percentages by incorporating Pepco’s actual historical

 6          net salvage data for the period 2005 through 2025. The net salvage percentages in the

 7          Depreciation Study are based on a combination of statistical analyses and informed

 8          judgment. For the net salvage analysis, cost of removal, gross salvage and net salvage

 9          are expressed as a percentage of retirements. The statistical analyses consider the cost of

10          removal and gross salvage ratios to the associated retirements during the 20-year period

11          for which net salvage data were available. Trends of such data are also measured based

12          on three-year moving averages and the most recent five-year indications.

13   Q35. How do Pepco’s historical net salvage results support your recommended

14          estimates?

15   A35.          Pepco’s historical experience demonstrates that the retirement of transmission

16          property results in material costs of removal and that those costs generally exceed the

17          gross salvage realized from retired property. I analyzed the Company’s recorded

18          retirements, cost of removal and gross salvage for the period 2005 through 2025. I

19          considered the overall historical experience as well as annual results, three-year moving

20          averages and the most recent five-year indications.

21                 The historical results generally support negative net salvage estimates for Pepco’s

22          transmission property. Importantly, however, I did not simply adopt the historical

 1          averages and, similar to the service life estimates, exercised judgment to develop

 2          estimates that best represent the future net salvage for the studied assets. Historical net

 3          salvage can vary from year to year depending on the nature and magnitude of the property

 4          retired and the work associated with its removal. My recommendations therefore reflect

 5          the historical evidence while also considering the expected characteristics of future

 6          retirements and experience for comparable electric utility property.

 7   Q36. Is a trend to more negative net salvage consistent with the experience of others in

 8          the industry?

 9   A36.          Yes. In my experience, many utilities have experienced a trend to more negative

10          net salvage over the last two decades. The combination of higher labor costs, increased

11          work requirements, more stringent safety and environmental requirements, equipment

12          costs, more complex permitting and traffic control, and work in congested or constrained

13          locations has increased the cost to retire utility transmission assets. Pepco’s experience

14          of increasing negative net salvage is consistent with other similarly situated utilities.

15   Q37. Were the statistical analyses of net salvage in the depreciation study based on widely

16          accepted methods?

17   A37.          Yes. The analysis of net salvage as a percentage of historical retirements is

18          widely accepted in the industry and supported by depreciation textbooks such as the

19          National Association of Regulatory Utility Commissioners’ Public Utility Depreciation

20          Practices. Because the net salvage estimates are percentages that are applied to the total

21          future retirements (i.e., plant currently in service), analyzing net salvage as a percentage

22          of historical retirements provides a reasonable basis for developing estimates of future

 2          salvage.

 3   Q38. Please describe the process that you used in the Depreciation Study to calculate

 4          composite remaining lives and annual depreciation accrual rates.

 5   A38.          After I estimated the service life and net salvage characteristics for each

 6          depreciable property group, I calculated the annual depreciation accrual rates for each

 7          group based on the straight line remaining life method, using remaining lives weighted

 8          consistent with the average service life procedure. The annual depreciation accrual rates

 9          were developed as of December 31, 2025.

10   Q39. Please describe the straight line remaining life method of depreciation.

11   A39.          The straight line remaining life method of depreciation allocates the original cost

12          of the property, less accumulated depreciation, less future net salvage, in equal amounts

13          to each year of remaining service life.

14   Q40. Please describe the average service life procedure for calculating remaining life

15          accrual rates.

16   A40.          The average service life procedure defines the group for which the remaining life

17          annual accrual is determined. Under this procedure, the annual accrual rate is determined

18          for the entire group or account based on its average remaining life and this rate is applied

19          to the surviving balance of the group’s cost. The average remaining life of the group is

20          calculated by first dividing the future book accruals (original cost less allocated book

21          reserve less future net salvage) by the average remaining life for each vintage. The

22          average remaining life for each vintage is derived from the area under the survivor curve




                                                      18
                                                                                       Attachment C
                                                                                      Witness Allis
 1          between the attained age of the vintage and the maximum age. Then, the sum of the

 2          future book accruals is divided by the sum of the annual accruals to determine the average

 3          remaining life of the entire group for use in calculating the annual depreciation accrual

 4          rate.

10          survivor characteristics of this property group. I compiled plant accounting data from

11          1999 through 2025 and analyzed the data for periods that best represent the overall

17          interval. Consequently, the retirement ratio is 0.0004 ($428,245/$1,196,477,191) and the

18          survivor ratio is .9996 (1-.0004). The percent surviving at age 1.5 of 99.97 percent is

19          multiplied by the survivor ratio of 0.9996 to derive the percent surviving at age 2.5 of

20          99.94 percent. This process continues for the remaining age intervals for which plant

21          was exposed to retirement during the period 1999-2025. The resultant life table, or

                                 PART I. INTRODUCTION

SCOPE

         This report presents the results of the depreciation study prepared for the electric

transmission assets of Potomac Electric Power Company (“Pepco” or “Company”) as

applied to electric transmission plant in service as of December 31, 2025. The rates and

amounts are based on the straight line remaining life method of depreciation.       The report

BASIS OF THE STUDY

Depreciation

       Depreciation, in public utility regulation, is the loss in service value not restored by

current maintenance, incurred in connection with the consumption or prospectiv e

retirement of utility plant in the course of service from causes which are known to be in

current operation and against which the utility is not protected by insurance. Among

causes to be given consideration are wear and tear, deterioration, action of the elements,

inadequacy, obsolescence, changes in the art, changes in demand, and the requirements

of public authorities.

       Depreciation, as used in accounting, is a method of distributing fixed capital costs,

less net salvage, over a period of time by allocating annual amounts to expense. Each

annual amount of such depreciation expense is part of that year's total cost of providing

utility service. Normally, the period of time over which the fixed capital cost is allocated

to the cost of service is equal to the period of time over which an item renders service,

that is, the item's service life. The most prevalent method of allocation is to distribute an

equal amount of cost to each year of service life. This method is known as the straight

line method of depreciation.

       For all accounts, the annual depreciation was calculated by the straight line

remaining life method using the average service life procedure. The calculated annual

and accrued depreciation were based on attained ages of plant in service and the

estimated service life and net salvage characteristics of each depreciable group.

                    PART II. ESTIMATION OF SURVIVOR CURVES

       The calculation of annual depreciation based on the straight line method requires

the estimation of survivor curves and the selection of group depreciation procedures. The

estimation of survivor curves is discussed below, and the development of net salvage is

discussed in later sections of this report.


SURVIVOR CURVES

       The use of an average service life for a property group implies that the various

units in the group have different lives.      Thus, the average life may be obtained by

determining the separate lives of each of the units or by constructing a survivor curve by

plotting the number of units which survive at successive ages.

       The survivor curve graphically depicts the amount of property existing at each age

throughout the life of an original group. From the survivor curve, the average life of the

group, the remaining life expectancy, the probable life, and the frequency curve can be

calculated. In Figure 1, a typical smooth survivor curve and the derived curves are

illustrated. The average life is obtained by calculating the area under the survivor curve,

from age zero to the maximum age, and dividing this area by the ordinate at age zero.

The remaining life expectancy at any age can be calculated by obtaining the area under

the curve, from the observation age to the maximum age, and dividing this area by the

percent surviving at the observation age. For example, in Figure 1, the remaining life at

age 30 is equal to the crosshatched area under the survivor curve divided by 29.5 percent

surviving at age 30. The probable life at any age is developed by adding the age and

remaining life. If the probable life of the property is calculated for each year of age, the

probable life curve shown in the chart can be developed. The frequency curve presents

the number of units retired in each age interval. It is derived by obtaining the differences

between the amount of property surviving at the beginning and at the end of each interval.

Iowa Type Curves
       The range of survivor characteristics usually experienced by utility and industrial
properties is encompassed by a system of generalized survivor curves known as the Iowa

type curves. There are four families in the Iowa system, labeled in accordance with the
location of the modes of the retirements (or the portion of the frequency curve with the
highest level of retirements) in relationship to the average life and the relative height of

the modes. The left moded curves, presented in Figure 2, are those in which the greatest
frequency of retirement occurs to the left of, or prior to, average service life. The
symmetrical moded curves, presented in Figure 3, are those in which the greatest

frequency of retirement occurs at average service life. The right moded curves, presented
in Figure 4, are those in which the greatest frequency occurs to the right of, or after,
average service life. The origin moded curves, presented in Figure 5, are those in which

the greatest frequency of retirement occurs at the origin, or immediately after age zero.
The letter designation of each family of curves (L, S, R or O) represents the location of
the mode of the associated frequency curve with respect to the average service life. The

numbers represent the relative heights of the modes of the frequency curves within each
family. A higher number designates a higher mode curve.
       The Iowa curves were developed at the Iowa State College Engineering

Experiment Station through an extensive process of observation and classification of the
ages at which industrial property had been retired. A report of the study which resulted
in the classification of property survivor characteristics into 18 type curves, which

constitute three of the four families, was published in 1935 in the form of the Experiment
Station’s Bulletin 125.

Retirement Rate Method of Analysis
       The retirement rate method is an actuarial method of deriving survivor curves using
the average rates at which property of each age group is retired. The method relates to

property groups for which aged accounting experience is available and is the method
used to develop the original stub survivor curves in this study. The method (also known
as the annual rate method) is illustrated through the use of an example in the following

text and is also explained in several publications including "Statistical Analyses of
Industrial Property Retirements," 2 "Engineering Valuation and Depreciation," 3 and
"Depreciation Systems." 4

       The average rate of retirement used in the calculation of the percent surviving for
the survivor curve (life table) requires two sets of data: first, the property retired during a
period of observation, identified by the property's age at retirement; and second, the

property exposed to retirement at the beginning of the age intervals during the same
period. The period of observation is referred to as the experience band. The band of
years which represent the installation dates of the property exposed to retirement during

the experience band is referred to as the placement band. An example of the calculations
used in the development of a life table follows. The example includes schedules of annual
aged property transactions, a schedule of plant exposed to retirement, a life table and

illustrations of smoothing the stub survivor curve.

Original Life Table
       The original life table, illustrated in Schedule 4 on page II-16, is developed from

the totals shown on the schedules of retirements and exposures, Schedules 1 and 3,
respectively. The exposures at the beginning of the age interval are obtained from the
corresponding age interval of the exposure schedule, and the retirements during the age

interval are obtained from the corresponding age interval of the retirement schedule. The
retirement ratio is the result of dividing the retirements during the age interval by the
exposures at the beginning of the age interval. The percent surviving at the beginning of

each age interval is derived from survivor ratios, each of which equals one minus the
retirement ratio. The percent surviving is developed by starting with 100% at age zero
and successively multiplying the percent surviving at the beginning of each interval by the

survivor ratio, i.e., one minus the retirement ratio for that age interval. The calculations

       The smoothing of the original survivor curve eliminates any irregularities and

serves as the basis for the preliminary extrapolation to zero percent surviving of the

the vintages which have not yet lived to the age at which the curve reaches zero percent.

       Depreciation is inherently prospective. Historical retirement data provide objective

evidence of the service realized by the Company’s property, but necessarily reflect past

experience and, for property that remains in service, only a portion of the ultimate life

cycle. Therefore, statistical curve fitting alone does not determine the future retirement

pattern. The service life estimates reflect consideration of the statistical analyses,

exposures at different ages, the age and composition of surviving property, Company

operations and future plans, field observations, and experience with comparable electric

utility property. No single consideration was relied upon in isolation.

       For these reasons, consideration was given to Pepco’s current transmission

operations, planned capital projects, and the principal drivers of transmission investment.

This information is relevant to the estimation of service lives because transmission assets

may be retired for reasons other than physical deterioration or failure. Assets may also

be replaced or retired as a result of capacity requirements, reliability needs, system

reconfiguration, changes in voltage, obsolescence, or reconstruction of existing facilities.

       Pepco is undertaking several significant transmission initiatives. The Capital Grid

program includes development of a 230 kV backbone and loop into the District of

Columbia, including GIS at Takoma, reconstruction of 230 kV facilities to Takoma,

reconstruction of the Harvard and Champlain substations, a new substation at Mt.

       Historical net salvage experience is an important consideration in estimating future

net salvage, but the estimate for an account is not necessarily equal to either the overall

historical average or the most recent average. Annual net salvage results can vary

considerably based on the nature and magnitude of the property retired and the costs

associated with individual retirement activity. Consequently, consideration is given to

annual experience, three-year moving averages, recent experience, and the overall

historical period, together with the expected characteristics of future retirements and net

salvage estimates for comparable electric utility property. The resulting estimate is

intended to represent the net salvage expected over the future retirements of the property

currently in service rather than reproduce the results of any particular historical period.

       The historical data also provide perspective on the reasonableness of the

estimates. For several transmission accounts, historical net salvage indications are more

negative than the recommended estimates. In these instances, the recommended

estimates recognize the historical evidence of removal costs while moderating the

indications developed from the historical data based on consideration of the property

studied and estimates for similar property for other utilities. This is particularly important

where the historical results are influenced by relatively limited retirement activity or

individual years with unusually high removal costs. Similar to the approach for estimating

service lives, the recommended net salvage percentages therefore reflect the overall

weight of the available evidence rather than a mechanical application of a particular

historical average.

       When more than a single item of property is under consideration, a group

QUALIFICATION OF RESULTS

        The calculated annual and accrued depreciation are the principal results of the

study. Continued surveillance and periodic revisions are normally required to maintain

continued use of appropriate annual depreciation accrual rates. An assumption that

accrual rates can remain unchanged over a long period of time implies a disregard for the

inherent variability in service lives and net salvage and for the change of the composition

of property in service. The annual accrual rates were calculated in accordance with the

straight line remaining life method of depreciation, using the average service life

procedure based on estimates which reflect considerations of current historical evidence

and expected future conditions.

        The annual depreciation accrual rates are applicable specifically to the electric

transmission plant in service as of December 31, 2025. For most plant accounts, the

application of such rates to future balances that reflect additions subsequent to December

31, 2025, is reasonable for a period of three to five years.

incorporated statistical analyses of retirement data, discussions with management and

consideration of estimates made for other electric utility companies. The results of the
